articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and Issues New FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question (FAQ). This action updates existing guidance concerning transactions involving Venezuela, signaling potential shifts in the scope of permissible activities under the sanctions program.

The specifics of the amendments and the new FAQ were not immediately detailed, but such changes often clarify or modify the authorizations for certain economic activities or humanitarian aid. Entities engaged in Venezuela-related transactions are advised to review the updated guidance carefully to ensure ongoing compliance.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran and Cuba-Related Designations, Issues New General Licenses
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new sanctions and licensing actions targeting Iran and Cuba. This action includes new designations related to Iran and a specific designation concerning Cuba, alongside the issuance of new and amended general licenses and frequently asked questions.

While specific details of the designated entities and the scope of the new licenses were not immediately public, such measures often aim to further restrict financial flows and trade with the sanctioned nations. The inclusion of Iran and Russia in recent OFAC actions raises questions about potential additional constraints on energy and commodity exports or on shipping, insurance, and financial channels that enable those exports.

One notable designation is Cuba's Banco Internacional de Comercio S.A. (BICSA), targeted due to its ties with Iran's Karafarin Bank, which has been under sanctions since 2020. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated that 'Communist Cuba has been allowed to operate as an outpost for malign actors and terror groups — including the Islamic Republic of Iran, the world's number one state sponsor of terrorism — to target the United States.'

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-Related Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation. This action indicates a de-escalation of sanctions against a specific entity or individual previously targeted under the Venezuela sanctions program.

Designation removals can occur for various reasons, including a change in circumstances, a shift in policy, or a determination that the designated party no longer meets the criteria for sanctions. The specific entity removed from the list was not immediately identified in the announcement.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. These actions aim to disrupt the financial networks of those who engage in illicit drug trafficking and support terrorist organizations globally.

The designations underscore the U.S. government's ongoing commitment to combating these threats by cutting off access to the international financial system for those who facilitate such activities. Further details on the specific individuals and entities designated were not immediately available.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, Issues ICC Designation, and Burma-Related Removal
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics. Concurrently, OFAC has issued a designation related to the International Criminal Court (ICC) and associated general licenses, along with a Burma-related designation removal.

The settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics addresses apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations, the details of which were not immediately disclosed. The ICC designation and accompanying general licenses suggest a targeted action with specific authorizations for certain activities, while the Burma-related removal indicates a de-escalation of sanctions against a particular entity or individual in that region.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued a new Russia-related General License. This action provides specific authorizations for certain transactions or activities that would otherwise be prohibited under the comprehensive Russia sanctions program.

General licenses are often issued to facilitate humanitarian efforts, ensure the orderly wind-down of certain operations, or permit specific types of transactions deemed to be in the U.S. national interest. The details of this new license will be crucial for entities navigating the complex Russian sanctions landscape.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related Designations, Issues Iran and Amended Russia-Related General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations, alongside the issuance of a new Iran-related General License and an amended Russia-related General License. These actions signify a dual focus on increasing pressure on Iran while also adjusting the scope of sanctions against Russia.

The Iran-related designations aim to further disrupt financial and other networks supporting the Iranian regime. Concurrently, the new Iran-related General License may permit certain transactions, while the amended Russia-related General License indicates a modification to existing authorizations under the Russia sanctions program.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes and Updates Designations, Publishes Iran-Related Alert and Amended FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced several designation removals and updates, along with the publication of an Iran-related OFAC Alert and an amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question (FAQ). These actions reflect ongoing adjustments to the Iran sanctions program.

The Iran-related OFAC Alert warns that foreign financial institutions (FFIs) that continue to transact with sanctioned Iranian financial institutions 'could be targeted at any time without advance notification.' OFAC also amended Iran-related FAQ 156 to remove earlier language indicating that OFAC would generally contact an FFI about its conduct before making a finding that the FFI knowingly engaged in sanctionable activity. This alert forms part of Operation Economic Outcast, launched by OFAC on August 24, 2026, to cut off financial resources supporting the Iranian regime.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter terrorism activities. This action reinforces the U.S. government's commitment to disrupting the financial support networks of terrorist organizations worldwide.

These designations aim to isolate those who provide material, financial, or technological support to terrorist groups, thereby limiting their ability to operate and carry out attacks. Further details on the specific individuals and entities designated were not immediately available.

articles.headline: Bank of America Fined $11,662,930 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced a settlement agreement with Bank of America, N.A., resulting in a civil monetary penalty of $11,662,930. This penalty is part of a broader enforcement action against the bank for violations of anti-money laundering and sanctions laws.

Bank of America agreed to settle its potential civil liability for 475 apparent violations of multiple sanctions programs, including those targeting Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism. These violations occurred due to a combination of technical and human errors, such as channeling correspondent banking payments through blocked banks, allowing designated individuals to make payments due to poor sanctions alert calibration, and failing to promptly update watchlists.

The settlement amount reflects OFAC's determination that the apparent violations were non-egregious and largely not voluntarily self-disclosed. This penalty is part of a larger enforcement action by the Treasury Department, which includes a $1.2 billion penalty from FinCEN and a $750 million civil money penalty from the OCC.

articles.headline: OCC Imposes Record $750 Million Penalty on Bank of America for BSA/AML Failures
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has announced a record-setting $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A., for widespread and egregious violations of the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and its implementing regulations. This penalty is the largest in the OCC's 163-year history.

The OCC found that Bank of America's BSA/AML compliance program was deficient and ineffective, with its transaction monitoring system failing to properly monitor trillions of dollars in transactions. This led to the bank filing a large number of late Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs) involving billions of dollars, many of which had indicia of money laundering.

Despite a December 2024 cease-and-desist order requiring the bank to address its BSA/AML deficiencies, Bank of America failed to prioritize compliance and did not complete many significant steps needed to establish an effective program. The OCC emphasized that the bank's poor response to its BSA deficiencies was unacceptable, warranting swift and significant action.

articles.headline: OCC Assesses $350 Million Civil Money Penalty Against American Express for AML Failures
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has assessed a $350 million civil money penalty against American Express National Bank and its parent and affiliated entities for significant deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and Anti-Money Laundering (AML) compliance programs.

The OCC found that the bank's BSA/AML program suffered from systemic internal-control gaps, weak independent testing, and inadequate BSA/AML training. Specifically, the bank's risk assessment focused too narrowly on its demand-deposit business and did not sufficiently address the risks associated with its much larger credit and charge-card business.

This action highlights the OCC's continued focus on robust AML enforcement and serves as a reminder for financial institutions to ensure their risk assessments accurately reflect their business operations and that historical control weaknesses are addressed to prevent missed suspicious activity.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
